title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Memory — October 2026

studies.title: Professionals on TikTok push repressed-memory claims more than laypeople do
studies.ns_score_reason: vivid, timely and genuinely surprising about who is spreading memory myths, though it is a content analysis rather than a study of what viewers come to believe.
studies.the_study: Researchers coded 394 TikTok videos found under #dissociativeamnesia, #repressedmemories, #repressedtrauma and #traumamemories for explicit endorsement of eight "common sense" beliefs about memory drawn from an established memory-belief framework. The most frequently endorsed claims were that traumatic memories can be repressed and later recovered (24.1% of videos), that trauma memories return as flashbacks (9.1%), and that emotional memories work differently from ordinary ones (7.9%). Creators who presented themselves as professionals were significantly more likely than laypeople to endorse these beliefs — belief in repression especially.
studies.why_it_matters: The idea that the mind buries trauma and can later disgorge it intact remains contested among memory scientists but is being amplified on a platform with hundreds of millions of young users, apparently with the authority of people claiming clinical credentials.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a scroll — a therapist in a ring light explaining that your body is keeping score of a memory you cannot access — then explain why memory researchers wince. The hook is the inversion: it is the professionals, not the amateurs, driving the claims. Worth calling Christopher Perez at Arcadia University, and a memory-distortion researcher such as those working on the recovered-memory debate for the counterpoint.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature for a general-interest or media-focused outlet on how the "memory wars" of the 1990s are being re-fought on short-form video, including how platform incentives reward confident clinical-sounding claims and what professional bodies can actually do about members who post them.
studies.caveats: Observational content analysis — says nothing about what viewers believe after watching; "professional" status was self-presented and unverified; hashtag sampling may not represent the platform; single snapshot in time.

studies.title: Letting your mind wander after studying does not seem to harm what you remember
studies.ns_score_reason: a well-powered preregistered null against a popular "quiet rest consolidates memory" narrative; limited by being online and short-interval.
studies.the_study: In a preregistered online experiment, 197 participants learned object-face pairings and then spent 15 minutes on either an easy (1-back) or demanding (3-back) task, with thought probes sampling whether they were on task, mind wandering, mentally time travelling, or blanking. The load manipulation worked — the easy task produced far more mind wandering — but memory for the pairs, tested immediately and after the delay, did not differ between conditions, and no mental state correlated with retention. An extra non-preregistered condition using a simple perceptual filler task gave the same answer.
studies.why_it_matters: It pushes back on the increasingly popular claim that the mind needs undistracted idle time straight after learning to lock memories in — at least over short intervals. Not a definitive refutation, but a solid data point for a literature that has been drifting on mixed results.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the advice readers have probably absorbed — don't check your phone right after revising, give your brain quiet time — and the finding that a well-powered preregistered test cannot find the effect. Open on a student deliberately staring out of a window after a study session. Call Philippe Blondé at Jagiellonian University, and pair him with a proponent of post-encoding "offline" consolidation.
studies.wider_angle: A craft piece for a research-culture or stats-literate outlet on why null results like this matter: a nice case study in preregistration catching an effect that the published literature had made look real, and how "mixed evidence" fields quietly resolve.
studies.caveats: Online, unsupervised sample; retention interval only 15 minutes, so says nothing about overnight or multi-day consolidation; thought probes are self-reported; absence of evidence in one paradigm is not proof of no effect.

studies.title: The promise of a reward sharpens memory in older adults just as much as in the young
studies.ns_score_reason: a cheerful, picturable result about aging memory with physiological corroboration, but the sample is small and lab-bound.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Twenty-nine adults aged 18-35 and 30 aged 56-73 completed an incentive delay task and a visual recognition task in which each trial offered no reward, money, or social approval, while skin conductance tracked sympathetic arousal. Both age groups showed the same pattern: greater arousal and faster processing when a reward was on offer, with money beating social approval, and better recognition memory — plus a richer sense of mentally re-experiencing the encoding event — on monetarily rewarded trials. In older adults specifically, the anticipatory skin conductance response statistically mediated the speed gain.
studies.why_it_matters: Given well-documented age-related changes in dopamine and arousal systems, the reasonable expectation was that incentives would lose their grip with age. They don't — which keeps motivation on the table as a lever in cognitive aging research.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the assumption that older brains are harder to motivate, then the data showing a 70-year-old's memory responds to a small cash incentive exactly like a 20-year-old's — and that their sweat glands give away the anticipation. Call Michael K. Yeung at The Education University of Hong Kong. Be careful not to pitch this as a memory-training prescription; it is a lab effect on recognition trials.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health or aging-focused outlet on incentive design in dementia prevention trials and rehabilitation — why adherence programs for older adults so rarely use the motivational machinery that demonstrably still works.
studies.caveats: Small N (59 total across two groups); single-center; cross-sectional age comparison rather than longitudinal; laboratory recognition task, short follow-up (none); healthy volunteer samples may not generalize.

studies.title: Making people feel lonely in the lab does not make them read hostility into others
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean randomized causal test that breaks a widely repeated loneliness story; limited by an undergraduate sample and a one-shot induction.
studies.the_study: 142 undergraduates aged 18-29 were randomly assigned to journal about a lonely memory, to a prosocial gratitude exercise, or to describe their morning routine, and then rated the intentions behind other people's ambiguous actions. The inductions worked — loneliness rose after the lonely-memory writing and fell after gratitude — and chronically lonelier participants did show more hostile attributions at baseline. But the induced swings in momentary loneliness produced no corresponding change in hostile attribution bias, with no interaction with baseline loneliness.
studies.why_it_matters: The dominant model says loneliness breeds social threat vigilance, which breeds more loneliness — a self-feeding loop. This suggests the cognitive bias is a stable trait-level feature, not something that rides on how lonely you feel this afternoon, which matters for how loneliness interventions are designed.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the loop everyone has read about — loneliness makes you suspicious, suspicion makes you lonelier — and a randomized test that cannot make the first link happen. Open on the journaling task itself: writing about a lonely memory reliably makes you feel worse, but apparently does not change how you read a neighbor who didn't wave back. Call Gabriel Norman's group at the University of Chicago.
studies.wider_angle: A policy-flavored piece for a public health outlet on the UK and US loneliness strategies: a lot of funded interventions target momentary feelings — befriending calls, social prescribing — when the cognitive machinery that may sustain loneliness looks more entrenched than that.
studies.caveats: Single-center undergraduate sample, unlikely to represent chronically lonely older adults; brief single-session induction with no follow-up; self-reported loneliness; vignette-based measure of hostile attribution rather than real social behavior.

studies.title: Words about food resist deliberate forgetting — words about death do not
studies.ns_score_reason: a neat, testable demonstration that survival-relevant material slips past the instruction to forget, but the four-experiment design and domain-by-measure interactions make it fiddly to tell.
studies.the_study: Across four experiments using the item-method directed forgetting paradigm, participants saw Spanish words rated for intrinsic survival value — drawn from two adaptive domains, obtaining food and avoiding death — and were told after each word to remember or forget it. Directed forgetting worked overall, but survival value cut across it in domain- and test-specific ways: in free recall, high-survival food words were recalled well even after a forget instruction, while death-related words showed a general memory advantage without disrupting forgetting; in recognition, the pattern reversed, with death-related words showing better recognition sensitivity after forget cues.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the brain's much-studied "survival processing" advantage is not one effect but several, operating at different stages — and that your voluntary control over what you let go of is weaker for some categories of meaning than others.
studies.pitch_angle: Open with the experience of being told to forget something and failing. The surprise is that whether you can succeed depends on what the thing is about — eating or dying — and on how your memory is later probed. Call Marcos Alonso at Universidad de La Laguna. Frame it as a window into how ancient relevance filters survive modern instructions, not as a memory hack.
studies.wider_angle: A longer piece for an evolutionary-psychology-curious outlet interrogating the survival processing effect itself: it has been one of the most replicated findings in memory research for 20 years, and results like this show the "why" is still unsettled.
studies.caveats: Student-heavy Spanish-language word lists, which may not generalize across languages or cultures; laboratory word-list memory is a long way from autobiographical forgetting; some effects are interactions across separate experiments rather than within one design.

studies.title: Parents' and teachers' verdicts on a child's self-control only partly match what tests show
studies.ns_score_reason: solid sample and a genuinely consequential measurement finding for developmental research, but the hook is methodological rather than a new fact about minds.
studies.the_study: 244 Hong Kong kindergarten children aged 5-6 completed direct tasks measuring inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility and behavioral self-regulation, while their parents and teachers filled in the Childhood Executive Functioning Inventory. Teacher-reported working memory difficulties tracked performance on all four tasks; parent reports tracked a narrower set. Crucially, parental education moderated the fit: reports from more educated parents lined up with children's task performance, whereas reports from less educated parents correlated with nothing.
studies.why_it_matters: A large fraction of what we know about children's executive function — the skills that predict school and later-life outcomes — rests on questionnaires filled in by adults. If those questionnaires work better for some families than others, the resulting literature carries a hidden socioeconomic tilt.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a parent ticking boxes on a form about whether their five-year-old "has difficulty remembering instructions" — and the finding that how well that answer matches reality depends on the parent's own schooling. Call Jin Liu's group at the University of Hong Kong. Resist framing this as "parents are bad judges"; the story is about what a questionnaire can and cannot capture.
studies.wider_angle: An education-press or data-journalism piece on screening tools in early years settings: which children get flagged for extra support, and whether instrument bias quietly determines the answer before any child is tested.
studies.caveats: Single-center, 97.5% Chinese sample in Hong Kong kindergartens — generalization to other school systems is uncertain; cross-sectional and observational; parental education is a crude proxy for whatever is actually driving the divergence.

studies.title: A deep thalamic region only starts telling danger from safety a week after the lesson
studies.ns_score_reason: first human evidence for a circuit known from rodents, with a satisfying time-delay twist, but small samples and the authors themselves call it preliminary.
studies.the_study: Adults learned to associate a cue with an aversive outcome on day 1 and returned 7-10 days later (n=28) for fMRI while the cues were re-presented. The paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus did not distinguish the threat cue from the safe cue during original learning — even though participants' sweat responses and expectancy ratings clearly did — but it did discriminate during the delayed recall session. A separate sample (n=56) confirmed no discrimination during acquisition or immediate extinction.
studies.why_it_matters: Rodent work has implicated this small thalamic nucleus in retrieving old threat memories; this is the first human imaging evidence pointing the same way, and it suggests the circuitry that stores a fear long-term is not the circuitry that forms it. Relevant to why exposure therapy gains can fade.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the oddity — a brain region that is silent while you learn to be afraid and only speaks up a week later. Frame around the clinical puzzle of fears that return after successful treatment, and why memories tested at 24 hours may be the wrong memories to study. Call Daniel Stout at UC San Diego / VA San Diego. Flag clearly that this is preliminary and not a treatment target yet.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a neuroscience or veterans-affairs outlet on the "24-hour problem" in fear research: almost everything we know about extinction comes from one- or two-day tests, while PTSD is a disorder of memories that persist for years.
studies.caveats: Small N (28 in the key delayed-recall sample); the PVT is tiny and hard to resolve at standard fMRI resolution, so the ROI is "PVT-centered" rather than definitively PVT; no clinical population; authors describe findings as preliminary.

studies.title: Angry and sad faces compete for different mental resources when you try to hold them in mind
studies.ns_score_reason: a careful dissociation with a control experiment, but tightly lab-bound and a hard sell beyond a short news item.
studies.the_study: Participants held one or three faces (happy, angry or sad) in working memory while simultaneously performing an auditory monitoring task set to low or high difficulty, then judged whether a neutral probe face matched an encoded identity. Two distinct effects emerged: loading up face-specific working memory hurt memory for negative faces more than happy ones, while loading general attention hurt memory for angry and happy faces more than sad ones. A second experiment with a perceptual matching task ruled out simple visual similarity and showed the attention costs appeared only when active maintenance was required.
studies.why_it_matters: It separates two things usually lumped together — "being busy" and "having a full mental workspace" — and shows they degrade your memory for different emotional expressions. A small but real advance in understanding why emotional faces are not all handled alike.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a crowded meeting or a noisy street: the person you are least likely to accurately remember depends on whether you are cognitively overloaded or merely distracted. Call Ricardo Basso Garcia at the University of São Paulo. Sell it short — this is a news-in-brief with a good visual, not a feature.
studies.wider_angle: For an applied-psychology or policing-focused outlet: what controlled dissociations like this imply for eyewitness accounts of emotionally charged incidents, where witnesses are both distracted and holding multiple faces in mind at once.
studies.caveats: Sample size not reported in the abstract; undergraduate laboratory paradigm with static posed faces; identity-matching with neutral probes is a narrow test; generalization to real-world face memory untested.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Causal tests that refuse to deliver the expected effect.** The previous run's cluster of nulls and reversals — "Your earliest memory dates from the same age whatever culture you grew up in" (PMID 42757868) and "A depressive bias doesn't stop your brain getting the usual memory boost from a sudden target" (PMID 42706587) — continues with two preregistered or randomized nulls here: "Letting your mind wander after studying does not seem to harm what you remember" (PMID 42771053) and "Making people feel lonely in the lab does not make them read hostility into others" (PMID 42831817). In both digests the null is the news, and in both cases the claim being tested had already reached popular and clinical writing.
- **Trauma-memory theory still failing its own tests.** "Intrusive memories may not be the simple conditioned reflexes we assumed" (PMID 42759257) undercut the conditioning account from the clinical side; this run adds pressure from two other directions — "A deep thalamic region only starts telling danger from safety a week after the lesson" (PMID 42843708), which implies the circuitry holding a threat memory is not the circuitry that formed it, and "Professionals on TikTok push repressed-memory claims more than laypeople do" (PMID 42847121), which documents how confidently the contested version is being broadcast.
- **Measurement validity as a running worry.** "Raised gamma brainwaves in autistic children track memory for faces over four years" (PMID 42721928) and "Decades after epilepsy surgery, most people say life is good" (PMID 42727324) both turned on what an instrument can and cannot license; "Parents' and teachers' verdicts on a child's self-control only partly match what tests show" (PMID 42166276) is the sharpest version yet, because the mismatch varies systematically with parental education.

**Advances**
- **Motivation as an encoding lever, with physiology attached.** "Choosing to act makes you remember better — and the brain signal shows it" (PMID 42753975) located the benefit in volition; "The promise of a reward sharpens memory in older adults just as much as in the young" (PMID 42849577), from the same journal, extends the motivational story to external incentives and shows it survives aging, with anticipatory skin conductance mediating the gain. Together they make a stronger case than either alone that motivational state, not effortful strategy, is where the leverage sits.

**Counterpoints**
- **The post-encoding window.** Last month's "Nighttime seizure activity may be stealing the memory benefit of sleep" (PMID 42748517), following the sleep and source-memory work (PMID 42492165), treated the offline consolidation window as a protectable resource. "Letting your mind wander after studying does not seem to harm what you remember" (PMID 42771053) finds nothing over 15 minutes of waking filler — a genuine tension, though the timescales differ enough that it is a caution rather than a contradiction.
- **Single-session autobiographical inductions: sometimes they move downstream cognition, sometimes not.** "Talking yourself down after good news makes you read social situations more rigidly" (PMID 42727265) used a recalled positive memory to shift belief updating; "Making people feel lonely in the lab does not make them read hostility into others" (PMID 42831817) uses the same style of manipulation, successfully moves the feeling, and finds no shift in social interpretation. Worth flagging for anyone writing about state-versus-trait social cognition.

**New themes**
- Memory misinformation as a platform phenomenon (PMID 42847121) — nothing comparable in the previous digest, and the first item in either run to look at who is doing the telling rather than who is remembering.
- Content-dependent limits on intentional forgetting: "Words about food resist deliberate forgetting — words about death do not" (PMID 42844925).
- Emotion-specific competition in working memory: "Angry and sad faces compete for different mental resources when you try to hold them in mind" (PMID 42845027).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies in this batch converge on how little deliberate control people have over their own memories — and how far that is from what they are being told. Instructions to forget work unevenly depending on what the word is about (PMID 42844925); a well-powered preregistered test finds that deliberately resting after study does nothing (PMID 42771053); the thalamic region that distinguishes threat from safety stays quiet during learning and only discriminates a week later (PMID 42843708); meanwhile a quarter of TikTok videos under trauma-memory hashtags endorse repression and recovery, with self-presented professionals the likeliest to do so (PMID 42847121). The one lever that does move memory in this batch is not effortful at all: the promise of a small reward, working as well at 70 as at 20 (PMID 42849577).

**Why pitch this now:** Both the study-hack economy and the trauma-content economy sell deliberate mental acts — burying, retrieving, resting, letting go — as the way to manage memory, and the people with the most authority online are selling the most contested version; the lab evidence in this batch points instead to incentive, elapsed time and the category of the material.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the illusion of voluntary control over memory: what people are told they can do to their own recollections, what the experiments say actually shifts them, and why the gap is widest exactly where the stakes are highest — trauma. For general readers who have absorbed trauma-informed and revision-technique content, with clinicians as a secondary audience.

**Potential headlines:**
- Willpower is the weakest tool you have for shaping what you remember
- The memory myths spreading fastest online come from people with credentials
- Before you try to bury a memory, consider what the forgetting experiments found

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features (Mind)** — the batch supports a mechanism-led piece with a clear practical throughline, and the directed-forgetting and thalamus results give it laboratory spine rather than self-help framing.
- **The Atlantic** — strong track record on therapy culture and credentialed authority online; the professionals-versus-laypeople inversion in the TikTok analysis is the kind of detail they build a piece around.
- **STAT** — would take seriously the clinical-misinformation half: licensed practitioners broadcasting a contested memory model, and what professional bodies can actually do about it.
- **BBC Future** — well suited to the "what actually works" strand, pairing the mind-wandering null with the reward result in a piece about evidence versus study advice.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Memory — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-09 | **Studies reviewed:** 8
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-10-09

---

### Study 1: Professionals on TikTok push repressed-memory claims more than laypeople do
**PMID:** 42847121 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Sample (394 videos), hashtags, the three top-endorsed beliefs and their percentages (24.1/9.1/7.9 vs. 24.11/9.14/7.87), the professional-vs-layperson difference, journal, date and the Perez/Arcadia attribution all check out against the abstract. The Caveats correctly flag that this is a content analysis and that professional status was self-presented.

**Issue A. NS fit score of 7 on descriptive, uncontrolled data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — vivid, timely and genuinely surprising about who is spreading memory myths, though it is a content analysis rather than a study of what viewers come to believe."
- **Abstract says:** A descriptive coding study of 394 videos; creator status is "identified as laypeople or professionals" with no verification described; the conclusion is only that findings "confirm concerns about social media platforms serving as a possible source of misinformation about memory."
- **Problem:** The score rests entirely on an uncontrolled content analysis in which the key grouping variable (professional vs. layperson) is self-presented and unverified, and in which no viewer outcome is measured. The fit note itself concedes the main limitation, which argues against a 7.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — vivid and timely, and the professional/layperson split is a genuine surprise, but it is an uncontrolled content analysis with self-presented creator credentials and no measure of what viewers take away."

---

### Study 2: Letting your mind wander after studying does not seem to harm what you remember
**PMID:** 42771053 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N (197), preregistration, online format, 1-back/3-back for 15 min, thought-probe categories, immediate and delayed testing, the null on memory and on state–retention correlations, and the extra non-preregistered perceptual condition are all accurately reported. Blondé/Jagiellonian is correct. The headline is appropriately hedged ("does not seem to").

**Issue A. "Overturns prior research" novelty tag** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "Previous examinations of the relationship between mind wandering (MW) during post-encoding periods and subsequent memory consolidation has led to mixed results… These findings add to a growing body of mixed evidence."
- **Problem:** The authors position the result as another entry in an already-mixed literature, not as an overturning of an established effect. The body text ("Not a definitive refutation, but a solid data point") is accurate, so the tag is the outlier.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Well-powered null in a contested literature"

**Issue B. Magnitude of the mind-wandering difference** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the easy task produced far more mind wandering"
- **Abstract says:** "The 1-back condition elicited more MW, particularly involving mental time travel, while the 3-back condition increased on-task focus."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a direction, not an effect size; "far more" adds a magnitude the abstract does not support.
- **Suggested fix:** "the easy task produced more mind wandering, particularly mental time travel, while the demanding task increased on-task focus"

*Note (not counted as an issue):* the entry contains a stray duplicated field — "**The media check:** —" above "**Media check:**" — which should be deleted before circulation.

---

### Study 3: The promise of a reward sharpens memory in older adults just as much as in the young
**PMID:** 42849577 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Group sizes (29 aged 18–35; 30 aged 56–73), the two tasks, the skin conductance measure, the equivalence of reward effects across age groups, money > social reward, and the mediation of the speed gain by anticipatory SCR in older adults are all accurate. Yeung/Education University of Hong Kong is correct.

**Issue A. Headline generalizes a monetary-only memory effect to "a reward"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The promise of a reward sharpens memory in older adults just as much as in the young"
- **Abstract says:** "Regarding memory, both age groups showed improved visual recognition and a greater ability to mentally re-experience past events when monetary reward was available."
- **Problem:** Speed and arousal responded to both monetary and social reward; the memory benefit is reported only for monetary reward. The body text gets this right ("on monetarily rewarded trials"), but the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "The promise of money sharpens memory in older adults just as much as in the young"

**Issue B. "Exactly like" overstates an absence of an age difference** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the data showing a 70-year-old's memory responds to a small cash incentive exactly like a 20-year-old's"
- **Abstract says:** "reward enhances older adults' processing speed and episodic memory similarly to those of younger adults, despite potentially different contributions of sympathetic arousal."
- **Problem:** "Exactly like" claims equivalence from a non-significant age interaction in a 59-person study, and the abstract explicitly notes the underlying physiology may differ. The reward amount ("small cash") is also not given in the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "the data showing older adults' memory responds to a monetary incentive about as much as younger adults' does — though the authors note the underlying arousal contributions may differ"

**Issue C. Wider angle asserts real-world efficacy** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "why adherence programs for older adults so rarely use the motivational machinery that demonstrably still works"
- **Abstract says:** Findings are from a laboratory incentive delay task and visual recognition task in 59 healthy volunteers; the stated contribution is to "deepen our understanding of the three-way relationship among reward, psychophysiological functioning, and aging."
- **Problem:** "Demonstrably still works" projects a small single-session lab effect onto adherence programs and dementia-prevention trials. That is an overgeneralization beyond the study population and setting.
- **Suggested fix:** "why adherence programs for older adults rarely exploit incentives, when lab work like this suggests the motivational machinery is still responsive in later life"

**Issue D. "Single-centre" claim not supported by the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Small N (59 total across two groups); single-center"
- **Abstract says:** Author affiliations span the University of Sydney, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University and The Education University of Hong Kong; no recruitment or testing site is stated.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — the number of testing sites is not reported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Small N (59 total across two groups); testing site(s) not specified in the abstract"

---

### Study 4: Making people feel lonely in the lab does not make them read hostility into others
**PMID:** 42831817 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N (142), age range (18–29), undergraduate sample, random assignment to the three conditions, the successful manipulation checks, the baseline loneliness–hostile attribution association, the null for induced change and the absence of an interaction are all reported accurately. Norman/University of Chicago is correct.

**Issue A. "Overturns prior research" novelty tag** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "While loneliness has been associated with increased hostile attribution biases, empirical studies have yet to assess whether loneliness directly causes increased hostile attributions."
- **Problem:** There was no prior causal finding to overturn — this is the first causal test of an assumption, and the correlational literature (replicated here at baseline) is unaffected.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** First causal test of a widely assumed mechanism — and it comes up null"

**Issue B. "Stable trait-level feature" goes beyond a null result** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "This suggests the cognitive bias is a stable trait-level feature, not something that rides on how lonely you feel this afternoon"
- **Abstract says:** "These findings have implications for the design of loneliness interventions, suggesting that targeting momentary feelings of loneliness may have limited effects on the hostile attribution biases associated with feelings of loneliness."
- **Problem:** A single-session null on an induced state cannot establish that the bias is trait-stable; that would require longitudinal or test–retest data the study does not report. The defensible claim is narrower: shifting momentary loneliness did not shift the bias.
- **Suggested fix:** "This suggests the bias does not track how lonely you feel this afternoon — the authors conclude that interventions aimed at momentary feelings may have limited effect on it"

**Issue C. "Vignette-based measure" not described in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "vignette-based measure of hostile attribution rather than real social behavior"
- **Abstract says:** Only that participants' "tendency to assume hostile intent behind others' ambiguous actions" was assessed; the instrument format is not specified.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "hostile attribution measured by self-report ratings of ambiguous scenarios rather than real social behaviour (instrument not specified in the abstract)"

---

### Study 5: Words about food resist deliberate forgetting — words about death do not
**PMID:** 42844925 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Four experiments, item-method directed forgetting, Spanish words rated for intrinsic survival value across the obtaining-food and avoiding-death domains, robust overall directed forgetting, and the free-recall and recognition patterns are all reported accurately in the body text. Alonso/Universidad de La Laguna is correct.

**Issue A. Headline contradicts the recognition result** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Words about food resist deliberate forgetting — words about death do not"
- **Abstract says:** "In the avoiding death domain, high survival-value words showed greater recognition following forget instructions, reflected in higher recognition sensitivity."
- **Problem:** Death-related words *did* resist forgetting — just on the recognition test rather than in free recall. The headline states the opposite as a flat fact, and a reader who stops at the headline takes away a finding the study does not report. The body text handles the interaction correctly, which makes the headline the sole problem.
- **Suggested fix:** "Food words slip past 'forget' in recall, death words in recognition — survival value resists deliberate forgetting, but not in one way"

**Issue B. "Student-heavy" sample description not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Student-heavy Spanish-language word lists"
- **Abstract says:** Nothing about who the participants were; it reports only that "Spanish words rated for intrinsic survival value were selected from two adaptive domains."
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — participant characteristics are not described, and the phrasing conflates the sample with the stimuli.
- **Suggested fix:** "Spanish-language word lists and a Spanish laboratory sample (participant details not given in the abstract), which may not generalise across languages or cultures"

---

### Study 6: Parents' and teachers' verdicts on a child's self-control only partly match what tests show
**PMID:** 42166276 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N (244), age (5–6), Hong Kong kindergartens, 97.5% Chinese, the four direct tasks, the Childhood Executive Functioning Inventory, the teacher-report pattern across all four tasks and the narrower parent-report pattern are all accurate. Liu/University of Hong Kong is correct.

**Issue A. Moderation by parental education is broader in the digest than in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "parental education moderated the fit: reports from more educated parents lined up with children's task performance, whereas reports from less educated parents correlated with nothing"
- **Abstract says:** "Parental education moderated the association between parent reports and direct assessment **for working memory**. Among more educated parents, parent-reported working memory difficulties were negatively associated with all EF tasks, and parent-reported inhibition difficulties were negatively associated with the inhibitory control task."
- **Problem:** The formal moderation is reported for the working memory scale only, and among more-educated parents the inhibition reports tracked just one task, not performance generally. The second half of the sentence (less-educated parents' reports associated with nothing) is accurate.
- **Suggested fix:** "parental education moderated the fit for working memory: among more educated parents, reported working memory difficulties tracked all four tasks (and reported inhibition difficulties tracked inhibitory control), whereas reports from less educated parents were associated with no task at all"

**Issue B. Publication date sits outside the stated coverage window** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Journal:** *Psychological Assessment* | **Published:** October 2026"
- **Abstract says:** "Psychol Assess. 2026 Oct;38(10):744-757. doi: 10.1037/pas0001480. **Epub 2026 May 21.**"
- **Problem:** The paper first appeared online on 21 May 2026, nearly five months before the 9 October run date and well outside the "Last 30 days" coverage window advertised at the top of the digest. An editor needs to know this is an issue-date pick-up, not new research.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Published:** October 2026 issue (online ahead of print 21 May 2026 — note this falls outside the 30-day window)"

### Study 7: A deep thalamic region only starts telling danger from safety a week after the lesson
**PMID:** 42843708 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The Day 1 / 7–10 day design, n = 28 for the delayed recall fMRI sample, the absence of CS+/CS− discrimination in PVT during acquisition despite differential EDA and expectancy ratings, the discrimination during delayed recall, and the independent n = 56 sample showing no discrimination during acquisition or immediate extinction are all accurately reported. Stout/UC San Diego and VA San Diego is correct, and the Caveats correctly note the histology-informed, "PVT-centered" ROI and the authors' own "preliminary" framing.

**Issue A. "Storage circuitry is not formation circuitry" overreads the data** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "it suggests the circuitry that stores a fear long-term is not the circuitry that forms it"
- **Abstract says:** "a human PVT-centered dorsal midline thalamic region is sensitive to prior threat reinforcement during delayed recall, **while also showing engagement during acute threat-learning contexts**" — and in the n = 56 sample "overall PVT activation was greater during acquisition than extinction, regardless of CS type."
- **Problem:** The PVT *was* active during acquisition; what it failed to do was discriminate CS+ from CS−. The digest converts a difference in cue selectivity over time into a claim about anatomically separate storage and formation systems, which the abstract explicitly complicates.
- **Suggested fix:** "it suggests this region is engaged during learning but only starts separating threat from safety once the memory is old — hinting that cue-selective retrieval recruits circuitry differently from initial encoding"

**Issue B. Clinical relevance claim not supported by the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Relevant to why exposure therapy gains can fade."
- **Abstract says:** The findings "support future investigation of PVT-centered thalamic circuitry in the persistence, retrieval, and updating of threat memories, as well as in salience-related processes." No clinical population was studied and relapse after therapy is not discussed.
- **Problem:** The link to exposure-therapy relapse is the writer's extrapolation from a healthy-volunteer imaging study; it should be marked as speculation.
- **Suggested fix:** "The authors flag it as a target for future work on how threat memories persist and are updated — a question that bears on why exposure therapy gains sometimes fade, though this study did not test that."

**Issue C. "First human imaging evidence" not stated as a priority claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this is the first human imaging evidence pointing the same way"
- **Abstract says:** "whether the human PVT shows cue-related discriminability during delayed recall remains unclear… These findings provide preliminary evidence…"
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — the authors describe a gap, not a priority claim. Priority assertions are easy to get wrong and invite correction.
- **Suggested fix:** "the authors say it is unclear whether the human PVT behaves this way, and this is the first imaging evidence that it does"

### Study 8: Angry and sad faces compete for different mental resources when you try to hold them in mind
**PMID:** 42845027 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The Experiment 1 design (one vs. three faces; happy/angry/sad; concurrent auditory monitoring at low vs. high load; neutral probe identity match), both dissociated effects in the correct direction, and the Experiment 2 controls (featural similarity ruled out; attentional costs specific to active maintenance) are reported accurately. Garcia/University of São Paulo is correct, and the Caveats rightly note that sample size is absent from the abstract.

**Issue A. Participant and stimulus details not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "undergraduate laboratory paradigm with static posed faces"
- **Abstract says:** Only "participants performed a face working memory (WM) task"; neither participant status nor the face stimulus set is described.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — the undergraduate characterization and the "static posed faces" description are assumptions about an unreported method.
- **Suggested fix:** "laboratory face-memory paradigm (participant characteristics and stimulus set not reported in the abstract)"
